There's a hum in my kitchen at 3:17 AM. It's not loud. You would miss it in the daytime under the clatter of pans and conversation and traffic, but at night it is the only thing in the house that is still working without being asked to.

It's the refrigerator.

I stood there last night in bare feet on the cold tile just listening to it. It has made that exact same sound every night for seven years, since we brought it into the house. It has never had a birthday party. No one ever took a picture of it. No one ever says, "Do you remember when we got the fridge? That was a great day." We celebrate the things that begin. We rarely celebrate the things that continue.

I think about that a lot. We have a mythology problem.

We tell stories about invention. Someone in a garage has a eureka moment. Someone in a lab shouts. Someone launches something. We love the launch. We put the launch on television. What we don't put on television is year four, day 219, when someone has to re-torque the same bolt for the sixth time because thermal cycling keeps loosening it. That is not heroic footage. But without it, everything falls out of the sky.

Our world is held together by maintenance, not by invention. That sounds insulting to inventors until you realize that maintenance is also a kind of invention. It's just an invention that happens over and over again, quietly, in the same place.

Look at any city from a high window and you're looking at a miracle of continued agreement. The water that comes out of your tap traveled through a hundred-year-old system of pipes, pumps, reservoirs, and filtration beds that someone has to walk through every day with a clipboard. The reason you don't have cholera is not because someone invented chlorine once in 1910. It's because someone today checked the chlorine levels at 6 AM and again at 2 PM. 

The Romans understood this in a way we have forgotten. We remember them for aqueducts and arches, but their real administrative genius was cura. Cura aquarum — the care of waters. Frontinus, the water commissioner of Rome in 97 AD, wrote a two-volume report on the aqueducts not about how to build them, but about how to stop people from illegally tapping them with secret pipes to water their private gardens. His book is 2,000 years old and it's about maintenance fraud and asset management and sediment buildup. It's incredibly boring and absolutely the reason Rome could have a million people living together on seven hills without dying.

We want to live on Mars. I love that idea in the abstract. But I think we should send the plumber first. Because the first Martian colony will not fail due to a lack of rocket science. It will fail because the air filter got clogged with dust and nobody wanted to be the person whose entire job was to clean the air filter every single day for the rest of their life. The future is a maintenance problem.

We like to imagine old things as having been built better. "They don't make them like they used to." Sometimes that's true. More often, it's survivorship bias mixed with invisible labor. That 100-year-old house is still standing because 12 different people who lived in it replaced the roof, repointed the brick, rewired the crazy knob-and-tube, jacked up the sagging corner when the foundation settled, and painted everything three times. A house is not an object. It's a verb. It's a slow, expensive agreement between wood and weather and people who care enough to intervene.

There's a Japanese word I think about too often: *shikkari*. It's not as famous as wabi-sabi or kintsugi. My friend who grew up there told me it means something like "properly, firmly, reliably, with tightness." A shikkari knot holds. A shikkari person pays their debts and shows up. We don't have a good single English word for it. Our closest is maybe "steadfast," but steadfast sounds like a knight. Shikkari sounds like a maintenance worker.

We have turned maintenance into a moral failing culturally. If you have to keep fixing something, you must have bought the wrong thing. If your relationship needs counseling, it must not be true love. If your body needs physical therapy, you must be broken. We imagine that healthy things are effortless. A good marriage, a good car, a good body, a good career should just *work*.

But nothing just works.

I once spent a week with a bridge inspector. His name was Luis. He inspects bridges for a state Department of Transportation. He has a little hammer and a lot of opinions about rust. He taps concrete and listens for the hollow sound of delamination. He photographs a crack every six months to see if it's grown a millimeter. He has been watching one particular crack on I-90 for four years. It hasn't grown. That's his victory. He told me, "People think bridges fall down suddenly. They don't. They ask you for years if you will listen. Then they stop asking."

We treat our own bodies the same way. We want a breakthrough diet, a transformative workout. What our bodies actually want is consistent sleep, water, fiber, walking, stretching, and someone to look at that weird mole. The boring maintenance is the cure. The breakthrough is mostly marketing.

In software — which is where I spend most of my modern life — we learned this lesson the hard way. For decades we celebrated the launch. Version 1.0! Shiny new app! The press release! And then we left the thing to rot while we started building Version 2.0. Now half the internet is made of code that nobody wants to maintain anymore, running on libraries that nobody maintains anymore, written by people who left the industry. There's a famous xkcd comic where all of modern digital infrastructure is shown as a teetering stack, and at the very bottom is a single block labeled "some random project a guy in Nebraska has been maintaining since 2003." That is not a joke. That is literally how encryption that protects your bank account works.

The most critical software in the world is maintained by people who are tired and underfunded and who get emails only when something breaks.

There is a kind of holiness in that kind of tiredness.

My grandmother mended clothes. Not as a hobby. She mended because you did not throw away a shirt with a torn elbow in 1952. She had a wooden darning egg she would slide into a sock to pull the wool tight over. I remember watching her and thinking it was magic — how the hole would close. She never made it invisible. You could always see where the sock had been mended. A little constellation of new thread, slightly different. She wasn't trying to hide the damage. She was just making it whole enough to work again.

We lost that. We replaced darning with discarding. But now the discarding is catching up to us, piling up in landfills and in orbits and in our own psyches. We're starting to realize that the disposable world was an unusual, brief, fossil-fueled illusion.

And so there's a quiet return happening. People fixing phones with tiny screwdrivers. People learning to change their own oil again. People keeping sourdough starters alive — which is nothing but bacterial maintenance, feeding a jar every day. People archiving old video games because Nintendo won't. Librarians — God bless librarians — who are the patron saints of maintenance. They do not write the books. They make sure the books continue to exist and that you can find them. That is not a lesser calling. That might be the highest calling.

A library is a machine for fighting entropy at scale. So is a garden. So is a friendship.

I think about friendships. The myth says we just *click* with people and then we're friends forever. The reality is that friendship is administrative. It's remembering that someone's mom is having surgery on Tuesday. It's texting "hey, you went quiet for a bit, you okay?" It's maintenance. And the friendships that last decades are the ones where two people decided, for no glamorous reason, to keep doing the unglamorous check-ins.

Love is the same. You don't stay in love because you're magically compatible. You stay in love because you keep clearing the filter. You keep listening for the crack. You keep checking the chlorine levels twice a day.

There is no final state. There is no "done." That is terrifying to a brain that wants closure, but it is also incredibly freeing. If there's no finish line, then you don't have to sprint. You just have to keep walking, and tending, and tapping with your little hammer.

Years ago I visited the Ise Shrine in Japan in photographs — I've never been in person. It's one of the holiest Shinto sites. It's been rebuilt every 20 years for the last 1,300 years. The same design, same wood, same joinery, rebuilt from scratch on the adjacent plot. When they rebuild it, they are not making a replica. The idea is that the building *is* the act of rebuilding. The divine is in the continuity of care, not in the old wood itself. Which piece of wood is original? None. All of it. Because the knowledge of how to cut it and place it has been maintained.

That's what I want to get better at. Not launching things. Not starting things. But continuing things. Being a shikkari person.

So tonight at 3:17 AM, I went back to the kitchen and put my hand on top of the refrigerator. It was warm from its work. Vibrating faintly. I said thank you out loud, which made me feel a little crazy and also a little less lonely. 

Somewhere there is a person checking a water treatment plant. Somewhere there's a librarian reshelving. Somewhere there's a son calling his father even though last week's call was awkward. Somewhere Luis is looking at a crack, waiting to see if it grew.

None of them will be on the news.

But we are still here because of them.
